title: Hubble's panoramic view of a star-forming region

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This panoramic view shows 30 Doradus, also known as the Tarantula Nebula, the brightest star-forming region in our galactic neighbourhood. It is home to the most massive stars ever seen, and it sits in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, 170 000 light-years from us.

No star-forming region we know of inside our own galaxy is as large or as productive as 30 Doradus. That makes it a natural laboratory for studying how big, heavy stars are born and how they shape the gas clouds around them.

The picture is one of the largest mosaics ever put together from Hubble photos. It stitches together observations from two Hubble cameras, the Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, and adds data from the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope of the European Southern Observatory, which traces where hydrogen and oxygen gas are glowing across the region.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (13.41 x 10.73 arcminutes) and distance (170000 light years), the frame spans roughly 663 × 531 light-years. Its light set out about 170,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This mosaic combines Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and Advanced Camera for Surveys with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, whose narrow filters trace glowing hydrogen and oxygen. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate the glow of particular gases and the long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the nebula appears far richer than it would to an observer.
